title: Decoration

image.credit: National Gallery of Ireland, Ireland; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: An abstract, geometric painting on a tall wooden panel. It is made of shapes rather than recognizable objects, and its outline follows the shape of a traditional altarpiece.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: A tempera painting on wood made by Mainie Jellett in 1923, now in the National Gallery of Ireland. It is 89 by 53 centimetres. The source pages tag it Abstract Art, Geometric Art and Shaped Canvas, and describe it as a tall painting in the manner of a traditional pentagonal altarpiece.

descriptions.k: This painting is made of shapes. It is tall, and the top is not flat. Look for triangles, curves and lines. Point to a shape you like. Can you find two shapes that touch?
descriptions.g12: Mainie Jellett painted this tall picture in 1923. It is made of shapes and lines, not people or animals. It was painted on wood. Look at how the shapes fit together like puzzle pieces. Which shape do you like best? Why?
descriptions.g35: Mainie Jellett painted Decoration in 1923 using tempera on a wooden panel. There are no people or objects in it, only shapes arranged to make a pattern. The panel is tall and its outline is like an old altarpiece. Look at how shapes overlap and repeat. How does the artist make a picture out of shapes alone?
descriptions.g68: Decoration (1923) by the Irish artist Mainie Jellett is an abstract, geometric painting in tempera on a wooden panel. The source pages label it Cubist and describe a tall shape like a traditional pentagonal altarpiece. Jellett worked with ideas of rhythm and pattern instead of showing a scene. How do the shapes and the panel's outline work together? Use what you see.
descriptions.g910: Jellett's Decoration (1923) is a geometric abstraction in tempera on wood, and the source pages call it Cubist. Its tall outline recalls a traditional pentagonal altarpiece, which links a modern abstract language to a religious art format. How does the work use shape and structure instead of subject matter to create meaning, and what is the effect of the panel's altarpiece-like form?
descriptions.g1112: Decoration (1923) by Mainie Jellett, held by the National Gallery of Ireland, translates the fragmenting lessons of Cubism into pure geometric abstraction on a wooden panel shaped like a traditional altarpiece. Working in tempera also recalls older painting practice. How does the pairing of modernist abstraction with a devotional format shape your interpretation, and what evidence in the work supports it?

k.daily: Find a shape you like in the painting. What is it?
k.emotion: How does this painting make you feel? Does it feel busy, calm or happy?
k.observation: Point to a triangle. Can you find another one?
k.analysis: Which shape is the biggest? Point to it.
k.line: Trace one straight line with your finger. Where does it start and stop?
k.shape: Find a curved shape and a pointy shape. Where are they?
k.color: Which color do you see the most in the painting?
k.texture: This painting is on a piece of wood. How do you think the wood feels?
k.space: The painting is tall. Point to the top and the bottom. What shapes are there?
k.light: Find a spot that looks light and a spot that looks dark. Where are they?
k.meaning: There is no animal or person here. What do the shapes remind you of?
k.culture: Long ago, artists painted tall pictures for churches. What tall things do you see in your town?
k.technique: The painter used paint on wood. What would you use to make a picture of shapes?
k.personal: Which shape would you give a name to? What would you call it?
k.critical: If you could add one more shape to the painting, where would it go?

g12.daily: Why do you think the artist named this painting Decoration?
g12.emotion: What feeling do the shapes and lines give you, and which part gives you that feeling?
g12.observation: List five shapes you can find and tell a partner where each one is.
g12.analysis: Which shape does your eye find first, and why do you think it stands out?
g12.line: Find a long line that leads to another shape. Where does it take your eye?
g12.shape: Which shapes repeat in the painting, and how does repeating shapes make a pattern?
g12.color: How do the colors next to each other change how each one looks?
g12.texture: The painting is tempera on wood. How might that look different from paint on paper?
g12.space: How does the artist make some shapes seem to overlap or sit behind others?
g12.light: Where does the painting look lighter and where does it look darker, and how does that change the shapes?
g12.meaning: There are no people in this painting. What story could the shapes tell?
g12.culture: The shape of the painting looks like an old altarpiece. What does that tell you about where it might have been placed?
g12.technique: Why might an artist paint on a wooden panel and not on paper?
g12.personal: If you made your own painting of shapes, which shapes would you pick, and why?
g12.critical: How would the painting feel different if every shape were the same size?

g35.daily: Which part of the painting makes you think most about how the artist arranged her shapes?
g35.emotion: What mood does the painting create, and what shapes or colors help create it?
g35.observation: Choose one section and describe its shapes, lines and how they touch or overlap.
g35.analysis: How does Jellett arrange the shapes so that the painting feels balanced even though nothing is a recognizable object?
g35.line: How do straight and curved lines lead your eyes through the painting?
g35.shape: What kinds of geometric shapes does the artist use, and how do they fit together like pieces of a design?
g35.color: How do the colors next to each other make some shapes stand out and others blend in?
g35.texture: What do you think tempera paint on a wooden panel looks like up close compared with oil paint on canvas?
g35.space: How do the overlapping shapes make parts of the painting look closer and others farther away?
g35.light: How do lighter and darker areas make the shapes feel solid or flat?
g35.meaning: If shapes and lines can stand for ideas or feelings, what might this painting be saying?
g35.culture: The page says the panel recalls a traditional altarpiece. How might that old form change how you look at a modern abstract painting?
g35.technique: What would be the challenge of making a painting only from shapes and not from things you can see?
g35.personal: If this were hung in your school, where would you put it and why?
g35.critical: Some people say abstract paintings are not real art. What would you say to them using this painting as evidence?

g68.daily: How does the way Jellett organized the shapes in Decoration make you look at the painting as a whole?
g68.emotion: How do the colors and the sharp or rounded forms shape the mood of the painting?
g68.observation: Compare two areas of the painting. How do the shapes and colors differ?
g68.analysis: How does the arrangement of geometric forms create rhythm and balance on a tall panel?
g68.line: How do the directions of lines, straight, curved or diagonal, create movement across the surface?
g68.shape: How does overlapping and interlocking of geometric forms give a sense of structure without showing a real scene?
g68.color: How do the color relationships create contrast and harmony in the painting?
g68.texture: How might the tempera on wood give the surface a different look than a painting on canvas?
g68.space: How does the artist create depth and flatness together using only shape and color?
g68.light: How does the contrast of light and dark areas build form in a painting without a light source?
g68.meaning: What might the title Decoration suggest about the painting's purpose, and does the painting seem only decorative to you?
g68.culture: What is the connection between a traditional altarpiece shape and this modern geometric painting, and why might an artist link the two?
g68.technique: How did using tempera on wood affect what Jellett could do with her colors and edges?
g68.personal: What patterns or designs in your own surroundings does this painting remind you of?
g68.critical: The source calls this Cubist, though it contains no clear objects. What evidence in the painting could support or challenge that label?

g910.daily: How does Decoration use geometry alone to hold a viewer's attention?
g910.emotion: What emotional or spiritual tone does the structure of the painting suggest, and how does the altarpiece-like format influence it?
g910.observation: Examine the places where shapes meet and overlap. What do the edges reveal about how the painter planned the composition?
g910.analysis: How does the composition create rhythm and balance in a tall, narrow format?
g910.line: How do diagonal, curved and straight lines contribute to movement and tension?
g910.shape: How does the work build an abstract pictorial order from fragmented and interlocking geometric forms?
g910.color: How do the color choices and their placement build hierarchy and unity in the composition?
g910.texture: How might the use of tempera on a wooden panel give the surface a different character from oil on canvas, and how does that affect the work?
g910.space: How does the painting balance flat design with suggestions of depth and layering?
g910.light: How does the arrangement of lighter and darker passages shape how the geometry reads?
g910.meaning: How does the choice of an altarpiece-like panel reframe an abstract painting as something with possible spiritual or ceremonial associations?
g910.culture: How might an Irish artist in 1923 have used Cubist ideas differently from artists elsewhere in Europe, and what could explain that?
g910.technique: How do the materials and format link modernist abstraction to older painting traditions?
g910.personal: What does this painting make you consider about whether art needs a subject to carry meaning?
g910.critical: To what extent does the title Decoration help or limit your interpretation of the painting, and what would you call it?

g1112.daily: How does Decoration reconcile the analytical logic of Cubism with a pursuit of rhythm and harmony in abstract form?
g1112.emotion: In what ways might the interplay of geometric forms evoke a contemplative or devotional atmosphere without any figurative content?
g1112.observation: Choose a junction where several forms meet. What does it reveal about the structure and logic of the painting?
g1112.analysis: How does the compositional rhythm function in the absence of a focal subject, and what does it ask of the viewer?
g1112.line: How might the dynamic of line, straight, curved and diagonal, enact a visual equivalent to rhythm or music?
g1112.shape: How does the painting transform the fragmenting vocabulary of Cubism into a self-contained geometric order?
g1112.color: How do chromatic relationships generate depth, tension or harmony independent of description?
g1112.texture: How does working in tempera on a shaped panel connect the painting to pre-modern practice, and what is the significance of that continuity?
g1112.space: How does the work negotiate between the flatness of the panel and the illusion of overlapping planes?
g1112.light: How might light and dark passages operate structurally in a painting with no illuminated subject?
g1112.meaning: What might be gained or lost by giving an abstract painting the title Decoration, and how does the title interact with its altarpiece-like form?
g1112.culture: How might the work's place in 1920s Irish art, as an early abstract painting, complicate narratives of modernism centered on Paris?
g1112.technique: How do the material choices, wooden support and tempera, position the painting between craft tradition and avant-garde experiment?
g1112.personal: How does your own reaction to non-representational art shape your reading of this painting?
g1112.critical: What argument could you construct that Decoration is a devotional work and not only a formal exercise, and what evidence would you need?

teacherNote.context: A tempera painting on a tall wooden panel made in 1923 by the Irish artist Mainie Jellett, now in the National Gallery of Ireland. It is abstract and geometric, and its shape recalls a traditional altarpiece. The source labels it Cubist.
directions: Have younger students cut out paper shapes, arrange them in a tall frame and describe the pattern they made.
Ask students to draw an abstract composition in which repeated shapes create rhythm, then explain which shapes and colors they repeated.
Invite older students to discuss why an artist might combine modern abstraction with a traditional altarpiece form.
